extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and readers of 19th-century American history and indigenous policy
extracted.subtask_description: A historical-analytic chapter describing causes and mechanisms of the decline of Native American tribes in the United States and the policies and practices (treaties, displacement, assimilation) that shaped their fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two alternatives for native survival: War or Civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Savages of North America had only two ways of escaping Destruction; War or Civilisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that these were the only realistic exits: either military victory over Europeans (now impossible because of resource/technology imbalance) or assimilation into European modes of life. Gives historical context (attempts at resistance, why they failed) and notes that even when tribes attempted unification or reform, disproportionate resources of whites made sustained success unlikely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation requires fixing peoples to the soil (agriculture)
rubrics_metrics.description: In order to succeed in civilizing a people, it is first necessary to fix it; which cannot be done without inducing it to cultivate the soil: the Indians ought in the first place to have been accustomed to agriculture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that sedentary agriculture and intergenerational transmission in one place are prerequisites for sustained civilisation. Cites failures of Jesuits and Puritans to civilize wandering hunter groups because they did not stop their migratory habits; stresses necessity of changing economic base from hunting to tillage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunting/nomadic lifestyles resist civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all nations, those submit to civilisation with the most difficulty, which habitually live by the chase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that hunters' mobility and dependence on migrating game prevent the steady social processes needed for civilisation, and that hunters also culturally despise labor (considering it degrading), creating both practical and normative barriers to adopting agriculture and settled life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduction of European goods creates dependency and changes incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: The Europeans introduced among the savages of North America firearms, ardent spirits, and iron: they taught them to exchange for manufactured stuffs the rough garments which had previously satisfied their untutored simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows mechanism: new tastes without the arts to satisfy them forced Indians to rely on trade (furs) to obtain European manufactures; this increased pressure on game and resources and made subsistence dependent on marketable furs, accelerating decline of traditional economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: European settlement drives game away and forces geographic retreat
rubrics_metrics.description: From the moment when a European settlement is formed in the neighborhood of the territory occupied by the Indians, the beasts of chase take the alarm... The buffalo is constantly receding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses contemporary reports (Clarke and Cass, Volney) to document that settlement reduces wildlife, forcing Indians to move westward and causing large-scale displacement even far from the frontier (sometimes felt 200 leagues away).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forced migrations produce extreme suffering and cultural extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The manner in which the latter change takes place is not difficult to describe... They follow the traces of the elk, the buffalo, and the beaver... Hunger is in the rear, war awaits them, and misery besets them on all sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the human cost: starvation, exposure, family and social dissolution, loss of language, names, and national identity. Provides vivid example of Choctaws crossing the Mississippi in winter, and the self-destructive drowning of dogs following their masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. treaty/cession practices: inducement and exploitation at treaty-grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: When the European population begins to approach the limit... the government of the United States usually despatches envoys to them, who assemble the Indians in a large plain... they spread before the eyes of the Indians fire-arms, woollen garments, kegs of brandy, glass necklaces, bracelets of tinsel, ear-rings, and looking-glasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the method and psychology: assemble impoverished Indian families, display goods to excite immediate wants (women and children become importunate), exploit improvidence and short-term preference to obtain land cessions. Cites legislative reports and observers to illustrate pattern and moral critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Buying Indian titles as a substitute for conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of buying Indian titles is but the substitute which humanity and expediency have imposed, in place of the sword.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that paying for cessions (often pittance relative to land value) is an expedient replacement for violent conquest and has been effective in appropriating large tracts; gives examples of enormous acreages ceded for small sums and annual payments (Osages, Quapaws), and cites congressional reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian improvidence and immediate-gratification preferences explain vulnerability
rubrics_metrics.description: Their improvidence is habitual and unconquerable. The gratification of his immediate wants and desires is the ruling passion of an Indian: the expectation of future advantages seldom produces much effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to explain why treaty inducements and goods were effective: cultural tendency to favor immediate consumption over future benefits makes long-term bargains (land cessions) attractive under pressure; legislative reports describe traders and envoys exploiting this tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed-race (half-blood) populations facilitate cultural change
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of European habits has been remarkably accelerated among these Indians by the mixed race which has sprung up. Deriving intelligence from the father's side, without entirely losing the savage customs of the mother, the half-blood forms the natural link between civilisation and barbarism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that mixed-ancestry individuals act as cultural bridges, spreading European habits and accelerating modification of savage states where they multiply; offers historical causes (e.g., marriages during wars) and notes uneven geographic influence (French vs English settlers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of successful adoption: Cherokee indicators of civilisation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cherokees went further; they created a written language; established a permanent form of government; and... set up a newspaper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents Cherokee developments (agriculture, written language, governance, press) as evidence that Indians are capable of civilisation, but cautions that such successes do not prove universal or inevitable assimilation given structural obstacles described elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civilisation by foreign enlightenment rarely produces equality; internal development matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Barbarous nations have raised themselves to civilisation by degrees, and by their own efforts. Whenever they derived knowledge from a foreign people, they stood toward it in the relation of conquerors, not of a conquered nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares historical cases (invasions of Rome, China by northern peoples) to argue that sustainable civilisation typically arises when barbarians are in a position of power relative to the source of knowledge. Implies that adoption of foreign civilization from a subordinated position tends not to produce equal standing.
